name: Uradhi, Angkamuthi dialect
confidence_why: Crowley's 1983 grammar of the Uradhi dialects, which covers Angkamuthi at first hand, gives antepenultimate stress with long vowels attracting primary stress, whereas StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz and van der Hulst 2014) codes Uradhi as fixed second-syllable stress from a one-line rule in Hale 1976 that concerns a different Uradhi dialect, so the placement is genuinely contested in the literature but the reference description is the stronger source.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry. 1983. Uradhi. In R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds.), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 3, 306-428. Canberra: ANU Press / Amsterdam: John Benjamins. ANU Open Research digitisation hdl:1885/114846 (https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/server/api/core/bitstreams/c04a4a25-bf4d-40bb-8f54-a5a13f9f443a/content).
catalog_locator: Section 2.3 STRESS, book p.322 (p.344 of the ANU digitisation); dialect coverage 1.2 pp.308-309; vowel length 2.1 pp.318-319
catalog_quote: 2.3 STRESS The stress rules throughout the Uradhi dialects appear to be fairly uniform. The most important generalisations regarding stress are: (i) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable, (i.e. third syllable from the end), of a word that contains only short vowels. Words of three syllables or less are therefore stressed on the initial syllable. Examples (from the Atampaya dialect): /áma/ 'person' /íku/ 'bandicoot' /íntinu/ 'story-place of brown snake' /túyuβa/ 'cigarette' /umúyanu/ 'nose' /ukúmala/ 'sweet potato' /ayparúmpiwa/ 'sparrowhawk' (ii) In the case of words containing long vowels, it is always the long vowels that receive primary stress, regardless of their position in the word. (Note that it is possible to have a word that contains two primary stresses.) The following examples (again from the Atampaya dialect) are chosen to illustrate this: /ití:na/ 'thigh' /amá:ka/ 'message stick' /tá:rá:namu/ 'reef-GEN' [p.318-319] In the Angkamuthi dialect, length is much less restricted, and even in underived forms there can be phonologically distinct long vowels in final syllables, which is not the case in the other dialects, e.g. /uyuwa:/ 'hard beefwood'
world_status: statement found in an open source

I re-extracted PDF page 344 (book p.322, header '322 Uradhi') with extracted text and viewed the saved page scan : section 2.3 STRESS reads exactly as quoted — 'The stress rules throughout the Uradhi dialects appear to be fairly uniform.. (i) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable, (i.e. third syllable from the end), of a word that contains only short vowels. new_statements.rule_in_words: In all three Uradhi dialects (Atampaya, Angkamuthi, Yadhaykenu): if a word has only short vowels, primary stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable (hence the initial syllable in words of one to three syllables); if a word contains long vowels, every long vowel carries primary stress wherever it stands, so a word may have two primary stresses.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; Crowley gives no statement on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the rules are hedged as 'appear to be fairly uniform' across dialects and 'the most important generalisations'. All illustrative words are Atampaya. Relevant for Angkamuthi: long vowels there are 'much less restricted' and occur even in final syllables of underived words (p.318-319, /uyuwa:/ 'hard beefwood'), which under rule (ii) would be final-stressed; lengthening suffixes (reciprocal /-:(t)pa/, reflexive /-:nti/, comitative -:yma, excessive /-:ta/) create stressed long vowels late in the word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain ('of a word', 'position in the word'); examples are citation forms. Note the pervasive word-final sandhi (2.4) alters surface syllable count at utterance end, which Crowley does not relate to stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley 1983 describes three 'Uradhi dialects' jointly: Atampaya (atam1239), Angkamuthi (angg1238) and Yadhaykenu (yadh1237); Glottolog 5.1 treats each as a separate language under Uradhic. The stress statement is made for 'throughout the Uradhi dialects' but every example is from Atampaya; no Angkamuthi-specific stress example is given. Angkamuthi differs in allowing distinctive long vowels in final syllables (p.318-319, e.g. /uyuwa:/ 'hard beefwood'), which by rule (ii) would carry primary stress word-finally. The catalog already holds the same passage under atam1239; this record extends it to angg1238 on the strength of Crowley's explicit 'throughout the Uradhi dialects'. Hale 1976 concerns the Uradhi-proper dialect (urad1239, Glottolog bookkeeping), not Angkamuthi.

For a vowel-initial trisyllable such as uˈtagak 'dog' StressTyp2 (Hale) gives second-syllable stress where Crowley's rule gives initial stress, so the placements genuinely differ. new_statements.rule_in_words: StressTyp2 classifies Uradhi as quantity-insensitive with primary stress on the second syllable from the left (2L, 'peninitial'). This is an abstract analysis (after Goedemans 1993) that posits an empty initial vowel in consonant-initial words; on the surface the rule it encodes is Hale's: stress the first vowel that follows a consonant, i.e. the first syllable of consonant-initial words (ˈjukuk, ˈminhik̪jik̪) and the second syllable of vowel-initial words (iˈpik, uˈtagak). The entry also lists Crowley 1983 as a source with the summary 'stress on heavy syllables, else on the antepenult', but that statement is not the pattern the database assigns.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress pattern: 'No information' (STC and SPC both 'No information').
new_statements.exceptions: A pattern row 'Exceptional (Uradhi)' exists but has no sources, passages, attributes or analysis attached; no exceptions are stated in prose. Remarks: 'An onset sensitive analysis can be found in Davis 1985. Our analysis is based on Goedemans 1993, and uses an empty vowel in front of consonant initial words (evidence; initial dropping), which is EM like normal initial vowels.' Theo_source: 'Davis 1985, (our book), Goedemans 1993'.
new_statements.identity_note: StressTyp2's 'Uradhi' is the language-level entry (ISO 639-3 urf, one lect, id 873), not specifically Angkamuthi. Its pattern and four example words derive from Hale 1976 (Phonological developments in a Northern Paman language: Uradhi), whose data is the Uradhi-proper dialect, not Angkamuthi; Crowley 1983, which does describe Angkamuthi (plus Atampaya and Yadhaykenu) and gives Atampaya examples for stress, is listed only as a second source passage. The StressTyp2 statement therefore bears on the Uradhi dialect group as a whole rather than on Angkamuthi in particular.

readall_conflicts: There is a real disagreement. StressTyp2 (the StressTyp2 entry for this language 'Uradhi') assigns a quantity-insensitive peninitial (2L) primary-stress pattern, built from Hale 1976:44 'Stress the first postconsonantal vowel in a word' with an abstract empty initial vowel (Goedemans 1993), and illustrates it with ˈjukuk 'tree', iˈpik 'water', ˈminhik̪jik̪ 'bird', uˈtagak 'dog' (initial stress in consonant-initial words, second-syllable stress in vowel-initial words). The catalog record and existing statement follow Crowley 1983 (section 2.3, p.322): antepenultimate stress in words with only short vowels (hence initial stress in words of three syllables or fewer, including vowel-initial ones such as /ˈama/ 'person'), long vowels attracting primary stress wherever they are; StressTyp2 even quotes this Crowley rule ('Stress on heavy syllables, else on the antepenult') as its second source passage without reconciling it with the 2L pattern. The two rules diverge on vowel-initial words (Hale: second syllable; Crowley: initial/antepenult) and on weight (Hale/StressTyp2: none stated; Crowley: long vowels stressed). Because Crowley 1983 explicitly covers the Angkamuthi dialect (with Atampaya and Yadhaykenu) and states the stress rules are uniform across the Uradhi dialects, whereas Hale 1976 describes Uradhi proper and StressTyp2's placement is a theory-driven reanalysis, the catalog's weight-sensitive antepenult reading remains the best supported for angg1238; the StressTyp2 entry…
